details:
**Medea**
Euripides's most famous tragedy, set in Corinth, in which the Colchian sorceress Medea takes revenge on her husband Jason after he abandons her to marry Glauce, daughter of King Creon. She sends Glauce a poisoned robe and golden crown that burn her and Creon to death, kills her own children, and escapes in a dragon-drawn chariot sent by her grandfather Helios.

**The Bacchae**
A tragedy in which Dionysus returns to Thebes to punish his family for denying his divinity and slandering his mother Semele. When King Pentheus tries to chain him, Dionysus leaves him tying up a bull, then persuades him to dress as a woman to spy on the maenads from a pine tree; the maenads, led by Pentheus's mother Agave, mistake him for a mountain lion and tear him apart, and Agave carries home his head.

**The Trojan Women**
A tragedy about the captive women of Troy after its fall, including Hecuba, Cassandra, and Andromache. The Greek herald Talthybius announces their fates and that Andromache's infant son Astyanax will be thrown from the walls; the boy is buried on the bronze shield of his father Hector, and the play ends with Hecuba trying to leap into the burning city before being restrained.

**Iphigenia at Aulis**
Euripides's last play, in which Agamemnon is told he must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia to Artemis so the Greek fleet can sail for Troy, which leads to a quarrel with Menelaus. Iphigenia is lured to Aulis with the promise of marriage to Achilles; the play won first prize at the City Dionysia after Euripides's death, together with The Bacchae.

**Iphigenia in Tauris**
A play in which Iphigenia, rescued from the sacrifice at Aulis by Artemis, serves as a priestess in the land of the Taurians, where she must ritually sacrifice any strangers who land there. She recognizes two captured Greeks as her brother Orestes and his friend Pylades and escapes with them.

**Alcestis**
A play in which Alcestis agrees to die in place of her husband, King Admetus, a servant describing her as both alive and dead. Heracles, a guest who behaved drunkenly in the mourning household, repays Admetus's hospitality by wrestling Death (Thanatos) at her tomb and bringing her back.

**Hippolytus**
A tragedy in which Aphrodite makes Phaedra fall in love with her stepson Hippolytus, who has spurned the goddess in favor of the chaste Artemis. After Phaedra kills herself and falsely accuses him, his father Theseus curses him, and a bull sent from the sea by Poseidon frightens his horses, causing his fatal chariot crash.

**Hecuba**
A play about the Trojan queen Hecuba after the fall of Troy, in which her daughter Polyxena is sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles. The chorus of captive women curse the sea breeze that will carry them away, and Hecuba takes revenge on Polymestor for murdering her son Polydorus.

**Ion**
A play in which Ion, a temple servant at Delphi believed to be an orphan, is actually the son of Apollo and the Athenian queen Creusa. Creusa tries to poison Ion before mother and son recognize each other through the basket in which she had abandoned him as a baby.

**Electra**
Euripides's version of the Electra story, in which Electra has been married off to a poor peasant farmer. Its recognition scene with her brother Orestes mocks the tokens in Aeschylus's Libation Bearers, such as the matching footprints and lock of hair.

**The Phoenician Women**
A play about the war between Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices over Thebes, unusual for having Jocasta still alive during the siege. Creon's son Menoeceus kills himself over the lair of the serpent killed by Cadmus to fulfill a prophecy of Tiresias that Thebes will be saved, despite his father's attempts to stop him.

**Cyclops**
The only complete satyr play that survives from ancient Greece, a comic retelling of Odysseus's encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus. The drunken Polyphemus calls the satyr Silenus "Ganymede" and drags him into his cave.

**Children of Heracles and The Suppliants**
Two plays in which Athens protects suppliants. In Children of Heracles, Macaria offers herself as a sacrifice to fulfill an oracle given to King Demophon, and Iolaus captures their persecutor Eurystheus; in The Suppliants, Theseus helps Adrastus recover the bodies of the Argive champions who died attacking Thebes so they can be buried.

**Rhesus**
A play of disputed authorship, traditionally attributed to Euripides, set during the Trojan War. The Trojan spy Dolon disguises himself in a wolf skin and walks on all fours to sneak toward the Greek camp, and the Thracian king Rhesus is killed in his sleep by Odysseus and Diomedes.

**Reputation: Aristophanes, deus ex machina, and few victories**
Euripides was the youngest of the three great Athenian tragedians, after Aeschylus and Sophocles, and wrote around 90 plays but won only four victories in his lifetime, with another awarded after his death. In Aristophanes's comedy The Frogs, Aeschylus mocks his verse by showing that any of his prologues can be finished with the phrase "lost his little oil flask," and he was known for his heavy use of the deus ex machina. The German Romantic critics August Wilhelm and Friedrich Schlegel later attacked him as inferior to his predecessors.
